businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Confront the data-access problem first — without a route to invoice data at regional density, there is no product. 2) Explore partnering with an existing invoice/ordering tool rather than cold-starting the dataset. 3) Get legal clarity on consent to resell anonymised invoice data. 4) Test whether operators would actually pay over free USDA benchmarks. 5) Decide whether this is better pursued as a feature or partnership than a standalone company.

clarifyingQuestions: How do we get invoice data at regional density — become the invoice tool, acquire a dataset, or partner — given we don't own the flow today?
Would restaurants pay for SKU-level benchmarking over free USDA commodity data, and how much?
Is this better built as a feature inside an existing invoice/ordering platform (or a partnership) than as a standalone company?

ideas.title: Repricing Advisory-in-a-box
ideas.oneLiner: A productised advisory-plus-tooling offer that helps seat-based SaaS companies model, pilot and migrate to usage or outcome-based pricing without wrecking their existing ARR.

market.why: The tailwind is strong and timely: SaaS is a ~US$316B market growing ~19% a year, and pricing is visibly shifting off per-seat — seat-based fell from 21% to 15% of B2B software companies' primary model in a year while hybrid rose to 41%, and a February 2026 software sell-off erased over US$1T on fears that AI agents erode per-seat licences. The reachable market for a boutique advisory-plus-tooling offer is a fraction of that (the pricing-software category is only ~US$1.9B by 2030), but the demand is acute right now.

entry.why: Moderate. A services-plus-tooling business is cheap to stand up and needs little capital — but the barrier is credibility: selling an 'ARR-at-risk' migration methodology to CFOs and CROs requires a track record and named references the team can't yet claim, which is the real entry tax.

cost.why: Low startup cost — senior people plus a pricing-simulation/ARR-impact tool — and quick to first revenue if clients can be landed. The binding constraint is access to senior pricing talent, not capital.

saturation.why: Mixed. The market is barbelled: high-end pricing-strategy consultancies (Simon-Kucher, 2,000+ staff, which already pairs advisory with its own software) at the top, and self-serve billing/metering vendors (Metronome, Orb, m3ter, Zuora) at the bottom that don't bundle migration advisory. The gap — a productised, mid-market-accessible advisory-plus-tooling offer — is real, but partly occupied at the top by Simon-Kucher.

moat.why: Weak. Methodology is copyable, advisory relationships are people-dependent, and the billing-infrastructure vendors that own the implementation relationship could add a services layer. A proprietary pricing-simulation tool and a credible operator brand (published benchmarks, named outcomes) are the only realistic moats.

margins.why: Mixed. Advisory revenue is capacity-capped by scarce senior pricing talent; a software/tooling layer scales at high margin. Blended margin depends on how much value is pushed into the tool versus billed as bodies — an advisory-heavy mix keeps it moderate.

founderFit.why: The best fit of the team's recent ideas: management consulting plus finance/investment is squarely the skill set for pricing strategy and ARR-impact modelling, and the offer is services-led rather than needing a product-engineering team. The gap is domain-specific credibility — SaaS pricing is a specialist field with entrenched experts, and the team would be selling to software CFOs without an obvious track record in it.

risk.why: Moderate. Capital-at-risk is low (a services business) and the timing is excellent — repricing is a 2026 CFO emergency. Against that: advisory doesn't scale, 'migrate our pricing' can be a one-time project rather than recurring revenue, incumbents (Simon-Kucher, the big consultancies) are the default choice, and the credibility barrier is real.

businessCase.summary: A productised 'repricing-in-a-box' — a repeatable methodology plus tooling (a pricing simulator, ARR-impact and cohort modelling, metering-readiness assessment) that helps seat-based SaaS companies move to usage, hybrid or outcome-based pricing without destroying existing revenue. The timing is unusually good: AI agents are compressing per-seat licences, seat-based pricing is falling fast as a primary model, and a February 2026 sell-off erased over US$1T of software value on exactly this fear — so repricing has become a live CFO priority. It fits the team's consulting/finance strengths better than any recent idea, but it's an advisory-led business (hard to scale, people-dependent), the credibility bar to sell SaaS CFOs is high, and Simon-Kucher already blends pricing advisory with its own software at the top of the market.
businessCase.customer: Seat-based B2B SaaS companies — especially mid-market firms below the big consultancies' focus — whose per-seat revenue is threatened by AI-driven seat compression and who need to migrate pricing without churning existing ARR. Sold to the CFO, CRO or head of monetisation.
businessCase.market: SaaS is ~US$316B and growing ~19% a year, and the pricing shift is real and current — seat-based pricing fell from 21% to 15% of B2B companies' primary model in a year, hybrid rose to 41%, and a Feb 2026 sell-off wiped out over US$1T on seat-compression fears. The reachable market for a boutique offer is far smaller (pricing software ~US$1.9B by 2030), but the pain is acute now.
businessCase.model: A blend of fixed-fee diagnostic engagements, a subscription to the pricing-simulation/ARR-monitoring tooling, and potentially a success fee tied to realised uplift. Pushing value into recurring tooling — repricing is continuous as AI features evolve — is what turns a one-off project into recurring revenue.
businessCase.goToMarket: Lead with credibility: published pricing benchmarks and thought leadership (the proven playbook for operator-brands in this niche), then convert inbound into fixed-fee diagnostics and land-and-expand into the tooling subscription. Target mid-market SaaS underserved by Simon-Kucher and the big consultancies.
businessCase.costs: Low — senior pricing talent and the build of a pricing-simulation/ARR-impact tool. The binding constraint is access to credible senior pricing expertise, not capital.
businessCase.risks: Advisory is capacity-capped and people-dependent; 'migrate our pricing' can be a one-time project rather than recurring revenue; the big consultancies (Simon-Kucher, McKinsey/Bain/Deloitte) are the board-level default and billing-infra vendors could add a services layer; and the credibility to sell CFOs a revenue-at-risk methodology is the hardest early barrier. The timing tailwind could also prove a crowded, hype-driven moment.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Establish credibility first — who on or around the team can credibly advise SaaS CFOs on pricing, and can we publish proprietary benchmark data to earn trust? 2) Decide the wedge: pure advisory, or advisory as the front end to recurring simulation/monitoring tooling (the more scalable path). 3) Interview 5-10 mid-market SaaS finance/product leaders on willingness to pay and buying process. 4) Prototype the pricing-simulator/ARR-impact tool. 5) Map the partnership option — feed clients into a billing-infra vendor's rails rather than compete with them.

clarifyingQuestions: Who brings credible SaaS-pricing expertise and references — the entry tax here is convincing software CFOs, not building the tool?
Is this pure advisory, or advisory as the wedge into recurring pricing-simulation/monitoring software (the only path that really scales)?
Partner with a billing-infrastructure vendor (Metronome/Orb/m3ter) as the delivery layer, or stay independent and compete with Simon-Kucher and the big consultancies?

ideas.title: VisionPro Games
ideas.oneLiner: Build and sell 3D/spatial games for Apple Vision Pro on the visionOS App Store.

market.why: The bet is constrained to the smallest XR platform. Apple doesn't disclose Vision Pro sales, but reported figures are ~200,000 pre-orders and analyst launch-shipment estimates of ~60,000-80,000 units, and demand since has been widely described as 'struggling' and 'niche' at a $3,499 launch price (raised to $3,699 in 2026), with its roadmap recently scaled back and no near-term hardware catalyst. By contrast Meta Quest, the category leader, has sold 20M+ headsets — so a visionOS-only game addresses perhaps one to two orders of magnitude fewer potential buyers.

entry.why: The platform is open to developers — Apple provides the toolchain (Unity, RealityKit, Xcode) and App Store distribution, and takes only 15% of the first US$1M in annual proceeds under its Small Business Program — so there's no capital or regulatory barrier to shipping a game. The real barrier is the specialist 3D/spatial game-development skill.

cost.why: Moderate. Building a polished spatial game is a multi-month development effort but not capital-heavy, and App Store distribution is cheap. The real constraint is that revenue is capped by the tiny installed base, not the build cost.

saturation.why: Mixed. The native visionOS game catalogue is thin (a sign of open shelf space), but the broader VR-gaming audience — and the proven hits like Beat Saber (4M+ copies) — sit on Meta Quest's far larger base, not visionOS. You'd have an emptier shelf but almost no shoppers.

moat.why: Weak. A single game has no structural moat — hits are hit-driven and easily cloned — and the whole business sits on one vendor's platform whose roadmap was recently scaled back, so Apple's choices, not the studio's, govern the ceiling.

margins.why: App Store software economics are attractive per unit — a studio keeps 85% of proceeds under US$1M/yr (less above that threshold) on a zero-marginal-cost digital good. But a high per-unit margin on a tiny base is still small absolute revenue.

founderFit.why: General software-development capability helps, but spatial/XR game development is a specialised discipline the team doesn't yet have, and the platform itself is tiny — so team-fit improves only modestly and the ceiling is the market, not the build.

risk.why: High. The installed base is tiny and uncertain, Apple's Vision roadmap was recently scaled back (a platform dependency the studio can't control), games are hit-driven, and the team can't build it. Capital-at-risk is contained to a single game build, but the odds of a meaningful return on a sub-million-unit platform are low.

businessCase.summary: Develop 3D/spatial games for Apple Vision Pro and sell them on the visionOS App Store. Apple's developer tools and a favourable 15% App Store cut (under US$1M/yr) make shipping a title straightforward, but the venture is constrained to the smallest XR platform: Vision Pro's installed base is small (Apple doesn't disclose sales; ~200k pre-orders and ~60-80k launch shipments reported, with demand since described as 'niche' at a $3,499-3,699 price), versus 20M+ Meta Quest headsets. High per-unit software margins sit on a tiny base, hits are hit-driven, the platform's roadmap was recently scaled back, and the team has no game-development capability.
businessCase.customer: The small, affluent, early-adopter base of Apple Vision Pro owners looking for spatial games and experiences.
businessCase.market: Vision Pro's installed base is small — reported at ~200,000 pre-orders and analyst launch-shipment estimates of ~60,000-80,000 units, with post-launch demand widely described as 'struggling' and 'niche' at a $3,499-3,699 price, with the roadmap recently scaled back and no near-term hardware catalyst. The larger VR audience is on Meta Quest (20M+ sold). A visionOS-only game therefore addresses a very small market.
businessCase.model: Paid or freemium game sales on the visionOS App Store; Apple takes 15% of the first US$1M in annual proceeds (the standard rate above that), leaving the studio the rest.
businessCase.goToMarket: Publish on the visionOS App Store and rely on Apple featuring, store discovery and the small enthusiast community. With so few devices in the wild, breakout reach is hard and largely gated by Apple's editorial choices.
businessCase.costs: A multi-month spatial-game development effort (the team would have to hire or contract the XR engineering); distribution itself is cheap. The binding issue is that revenue is capped by the installed base, not the build.
businessCase.risks: A tiny, uncertain installed base on a single premium platform whose roadmap was recently scaled back; hit-driven game economics; the far larger audience being on Meta Quest instead; and no game-development capability on the team. Capital-at-risk is limited to the build, but expected return is low.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Confront the platform-size problem — get a dated, sourced Vision Pro installed-base figure and decide whether any visionOS-only title can pay back. 2) Consider building cross-platform (Meta Quest first, where the audience and the proven hits are) rather than visionOS-exclusive. 3) Be honest about the capability gap — this needs XR/game-dev talent the team would have to bring in. 4) Prototype a small experience before committing. 5) Check whether Apple funds or features spatial-game developers.

clarifyingQuestions: What's the actual reachable Vision Pro installed base, and can a visionOS-only game pay back against it — or should this target Meta Quest (20M+ devices) first?
Who builds the game? Spatial game development is specialist XR engineering the team doesn't currently have.
Is there a reason to bet on Apple's smallest, premium platform over the larger VR audience, given the tiny base and scaled-back roadmap?

ideas.title: Immersive Movies on VisionPro
ideas.oneLiner: Produce immersive, volumetric movies — where the viewer is inside the action and can change viewpoint — for Apple Vision Pro.

market.why: The same tiny Vision Pro base as any visionOS venture (Apple doesn't disclose sales; ~200k pre-orders and ~60-80k launch shipments reported, demand 'niche' at $3,499-3,699), with an added constraint: there is no open, paid third-party storefront for immersive films. Apple largely commissions and curates the marquee 'Apple Immersive Video' content itself, so a producer's addressable market is gated by Apple, not open to direct sale.

entry.why: High barriers on two fronts. Production needs specialist volumetric capture — the reference camera, Blackmagic's URSA Cine Immersive, is ~US$22,000-31,000 before rigs, crew and specialist stereoscopic/spatial-audio post — and there is no open self-publish route: reaching viewers means being commissioned or curated by Apple. Capital and access barriers are both high.

cost.why: High and specialist. A single immersive title is a high-capital production — the reference capture camera alone is ~US$22,000-31,000, before rigs, crew and specialist post — with no assured route to revenue, unlike a laptop-and-camera indie film.

saturation.why: The third-party immersive-film catalogue is thin, but that is because there is barely a market: the marquee content (Apple's own Elevated, Adventure, live NBA, NASA capture) is Apple-produced and Apple-curated, and only a handful of third-party titles (e.g. CANAL+'s immersive MotoGP documentary) exist. A newcomer competes against the platform owner for a curated shelf, not an open market.

moat.why: Weak from the venture's side — it wouldn't control distribution (Apple does), content is commissioned rather than owned-and-sold, and the format is Apple's. Specialist production capability is a mild skill barrier, but not a business moat.

margins.why: Poor for a standalone producer: high, specialist production cost per title against uncertain, commissioned revenue and no scalable self-publish storefront. This is project-based media economics, not scalable software.

founderFit.why: Very weak. Immersive/volumetric film production is a specialist capability the team doesn't have; a marketing/creative instinct is tangential at best to shooting stereoscopic 8K-per-eye content and mastering spatial audio.

risk.why: High. Large capital per title, no confirmed monetisation path (Apple commissions and curates rather than running an open paid store), a tiny platform whose roadmap was recently scaled back, and no in-house production capability. A produced title could have nowhere to sell.

businessCase.summary: Produce immersive, volumetric movies for Apple Vision Pro — 'Apple Immersive Video'-style films (180-degree stereoscopic 3D, dual-8K-per-eye, spatial audio) that put the viewer inside the action. The format is striking, but the business is doubly constrained: the Vision Pro installed base is small (Apple doesn't disclose sales; ~200k pre-orders and ~60-80k launch shipments reported, 'niche' demand at $3,499-3,699), and there is no open paid storefront for third-party immersive films — Apple commissions and curates the marquee content itself. Production is high-capital and specialist (the reference camera alone is ~US$22-31k before rigs, crew and post), the monetisation path is unconfirmed, and the team has no immersive-film capability.
businessCase.customer: The small base of Apple Vision Pro owners consuming immersive content — reached, in practice, only if Apple commissions or curates the work, since there is no open paid immersive-film storefront.
businessCase.market: The addressable audience is the small Vision Pro installed base (~200k pre-orders, ~60-80k launch shipments reported; 'niche' demand at a $3,499-3,699 price), and access to it is gated: Apple produces and curates the flagship Apple Immersive Video titles, with only a handful of third-party works so far. There is no confirmed open, paid market a producer can simply sell into.
businessCase.model: Unclear and gating: there is no disclosed third-party revenue-share or open storefront for Apple Immersive Video. The realistic near-term path is commissioned or branded work for Apple or partners (as with CANAL+'s immersive MotoGP documentary), not self-published direct-to-consumer sales.
businessCase.goToMarket: In practice, pitch Apple or brand partners to commission immersive content, since viewers are reached through Apple's curated app rather than an open store. That makes the go-to-market a bespoke-commission business, not a scalable publishing one.
businessCase.costs: High and specialist: volumetric capture hardware (the reference Blackmagic URSA Cine Immersive camera is ~US$22-31k), plus rigs, crew and specialist stereoscopic and spatial-audio post-production per title.
businessCase.risks: No confirmed way to monetise third-party immersive films (Apple commissions/curates); a tiny platform with a recently scaled-back roadmap; high capital per title; competition for the curated shelf against Apple's own first-party content; and no in-house production capability. A finished title could have no route to market.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Resolve the monetisation question first — establish whether Apple offers any third-party revenue-share or open publishing for Immersive Video, or whether this is commission-only. 2) If commission-only, treat it as a production-services pitch to Apple/brands, not a product. 3) Weigh the specialist capital (camera, rigs, post) against the tiny audience. 4) Consider the larger Meta Quest immersive-video audience as an alternative. 5) Be honest about the missing production capability.

clarifyingQuestions: Is there any open, paid route to sell immersive films to Vision Pro owners, or is it commission-and-curate only through Apple? (This determines whether there's a business at all.)
Given the ~US$22-31k+ specialist capture cost per production and a tiny installed base, what's the path to payback?
Who produces the immersive content — this needs specialist volumetric-film capability the team doesn't have?

ideas.title: AI Dating App
ideas.oneLiner: A dating app where an AI builds a detailed profile of each user and matches them with compatible people.

market.why: The online-dating market is sizeable — Match Group and Bumble alone booked ~US$4.5B of revenue in 2025 — but it is mature and softening: Tinder's paying users have fallen every year (10.9M in 2022 to 9M in 2025), Bumble's revenue fell ~10% in 2025, and dating-app burnout is widely reported. Crucially, a new entrant's reachable market is tiny — credible newcomers launch one city at a time — not the headline figure.

entry.why: Hard. Beyond building the app, dating demands a brutal, marketing-heavy customer-acquisition war and a two-sided local-liquidity cold-start — you need enough of both sides in the same city before the product works, which is why serious entrants (Sitch in New York, Overtone in select locations) launch one metro at a time.

cost.why: High. Dating is notoriously acquisition-spend-heavy (Match put US$50M of marketing behind Tinder alone), and reaching local liquidity in even one city is expensive and slow before subscriptions cover it.

saturation.why: Brutally saturated. Match Group owns Tinder and Hinge, the category's two dominant apps, and the exact 'AI learns you, curates matches, no swiping' concept is already shipping from incumbents (Tinder 'Chemistry', Bumble 'Bee') AND from Overtone — the founder of Hinge, who raised US$18M backed by Match Group itself. The specific idea is being built by arguably the most credible possible team.

moat.why: Very weak. Matching approaches are copyable, a newcomer has no data or network advantage at cold-start, and the incumbents (and well-funded AI-first entrants) already hold the users and the concept. There is no defensible edge on offer.

margins.why: Dating subscriptions carry decent gross margins and real ARPU (Bumble ~US$22/month per payer; new AI-matchmaking entrants charge ~US$20-30 per introduction), but success-driven churn and high acquisition cost erode the lifetime-value-to-CAC economics that actually matter.

founderFit.why: The team's in-house software-development and applied-AI capability, plus marketing, genuinely fits building an AI-matching app. But the decisive gaps are go-to-market, not build: outspending entrenched incumbents in a customer-acquisition war and solving the two-sided local cold-start — neither of which team capability resolves.

risk.why: High, with a sharp privacy dimension. An AI building a 'detailed profile' of personality and behaviour is exactly special-category sensitive personal data (orientation, beliefs), carrying the heaviest privacy obligations — and dating apps are already rated a category-wide privacy failure. Add trust/safety and AI-authenticity/deepfake concerns (an AI-mediated product can make users doubt they're talking to a real person), a marketing-spend war, a two-sided local cold-start, and the structural paradox that success (couples forming) drives churn.

businessCase.summary: A dating app where an AI builds a detailed profile of each user — personality, preferences, behaviour — and matches them with compatible people, reducing swiping. The problem is that this is one of the most hostile markets a new consumer app can pick: it's mature and softening (Tinder's payers down every year to 9M in 2025, Bumble's revenue down ~10%, widespread user burnout), dominated by Match Group (owner of Tinder and Hinge), and the exact 'AI learns you, curates matches' concept is already shipping from Tinder and Bumble AND from Overtone — the Hinge founder, funded with US$18M and backed by Match itself. On top of a brutal customer-acquisition war and a two-sided local cold-start, a 'detailed AI profile' turns sensitive-data privacy into a first-order legal risk.
businessCase.customer: Singles frustrated with swipe-based apps who want AI-curated, higher-relevance matches — reachable only city-by-city, since dating requires local density on both sides.
businessCase.market: Online dating is large (Match Group and Bumble alone ~US$4.5B revenue in 2025) but mature and declining at the edges — Tinder paying users fell from 10.9M (2022) to 9M (2025), Bumble revenue fell ~10% in 2025, and user burnout is widespread. A new entrant's reachable market is a single city at a time, not the headline figure.
businessCase.model: Subscription and/or pay-per-match (incumbent ARPU is ~US$22/month per payer; AI-matchmaking entrants charge ~US$20-30 per introduction). Revenue only follows once local liquidity exists.
businessCase.goToMarket: The only workable path is city-by-city: build critical mass of both sides in one metro before expanding — the model both credible AI-first entrants (Sitch in New York, Overtone in select locations) have adopted. This requires heavy, sustained acquisition spend against incumbents.
businessCase.costs: Dominated by customer acquisition — dating is famously marketing-heavy (Match spent US$50M on Tinder alone) — plus consumer-app and AI development. Reaching local liquidity is expensive and slow before subscriptions pay back.
businessCase.risks: Sensitive-data privacy is the sharpest risk: a 'detailed AI profile' is special-category personal data with the heaviest legal obligations, in a category already rated a privacy failure. Add a marketing-spend war against Match Group, a two-sided local cold-start, trust/safety and AI-authenticity/deepfake concerns, the same concept already shipping from incumbents and the Hinge founder's Overtone, and the paradox that success (couples forming) drives churn.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Confront the differentiation problem — Overtone (Hinge's founder, US$18M, Match-backed) and the incumbents already ship 'AI learns you, curated matches'; what is genuinely different and defensible? 2) Get privacy/legal advice on special-category data BEFORE building — consent, data-minimisation and lawful basis are gating. 3) Pick one city and model the cost of reaching two-sided liquidity there. 4) Be realistic about competing on acquisition spend against Match Group. 5) Consider whether a narrow niche (a specific community) is more defensible than a general AI dating app.

clarifyingQuestions: What is genuinely differentiated and defensible versus incumbents (Tinder 'Chemistry', Bumble 'Bee') and Overtone (the Hinge founder's Match-backed AI dating app) already shipping the same concept?
How is the sensitive-data privacy problem handled — an AI 'detailed profile' is special-category data with the heaviest legal obligations?
Which single city is the beachhead, and how is the two-sided local-liquidity cold-start funded against incumbents' acquisition budgets?

ideas.title: Proximity Social Game
ideas.oneLiner: A mobile game that pings you when another player is physically nearby and prompts a quick real-world interaction — rock-paper-scissors, a spy code word, a challenge — turning the strangers around you into live game targets.

market.why: Location-based gaming is a real but modest genre — roughly US$1.2B globally in 2023 (Japan alone ~US$620M, about half) — and it is dominated by games whose targets are virtual (Pokemon Go, Ingress), which sidesteps needing another live player nearby. Pokemon Go's scale (1B+ downloads) is the wrong benchmark here: its magic was ambient single-player-versus-environment play on pre-existing IP. A no-IP game whose targets are real people has a far smaller reachable market, and every comparable human-proximity social app has failed.

entry.why: A basic app is cheap to build, but the mechanic the idea wants is technically constrained: phones can't reliably detect arbitrary nearby phones in the background — NFC is a ~4cm touch technology with no peer or background scanning, and iOS heavily throttles background Bluetooth advertising/scanning between third-party apps. The workable path is server-side GPS proximity (the Pokemon Go model), and the real barrier is non-technical: assembling local player density.

cost.why: Building a GPS-plus-server MVP is modest, but there is no revenue until local density exists, and an app that sends users toward real strangers needs identity/age checks, reporting/blocking and human moderation from day one — real cost and friction. Acquiring users in dense geographic clusters (buying local liquidity, not diffuse installs) is expensive per active experience.

saturation.why: There is no durable incumbent in 'proximity real-world micro-games' specifically — but that niche is empty because it is hard, not because it is open. The proximity-social category is a graveyard: Bump (shut 2014), Color (wound down 2012), Yik Yak (shut 2017), Zenly (discontinued ~2022) all died, and no human-proximity social game has reached durable scale.

moat.why: Weak. The concept is easily copied; the only real moat is the player-density network effect — which is precisely the thing that can't be bootstrapped. Exclusive venue/event-organiser relationships (in the bounded-venue version) are a modest, more attainable moat.

margins.why: If it ever reached density, the economics are attractive and scalable — free-to-play in-app purchases plus paid real-world events (the location-gaming norm) on software-style margins. But that is conditional on solving density, and the mandatory safety/moderation overhead and the density ceiling temper the scalability.

founderFit.why: The team can now build it — in-house software-development and applied-AI capability, plus marketing, put the app itself within reach. But the binding problems here are not the build: the open-world consumer version still faces the local-density cold-start and the stranger-safety burden, where the team has no special advantage or consumer-scaling track record.

risk.why: High, on two fronts. First, a two-sided local-density cold-start in its most acute form — the game is nothing unless another player is within a few metres right now, the exact failure that killed the whole proximity-social category (Color, Bump, Yik Yak, Zenly). Second, safety and liability: pointing users at real strangers to meet in person invites harassment, stalking and luring (location games already have a record of lure-based crime; Yik Yak collapsed under cyberbullying), on top of a continuous-location privacy honeypot and platform limits on background location/Bluetooth.

businessCase.summary: A mobile game that alerts you when another player is physically nearby and prompts a quick real-world interaction — rock-paper-scissors, exchanging a spy code word, a challenge or task — a 'Pokemon Go, but the targets are real people' social game. A technical correction anchors the case: phones cannot sense each other by RFID/NFC as the pitch assumes — NFC is a ~4cm touch technology with no phone-to-phone peer or background scanning (Android's old NFC 'Beam' was removed in 2019), and even Bluetooth cannot reliably detect arbitrary nearby phones in the background (Apple and Google had to build COVID exposure-notification into the operating system itself for exactly this reason). The buildable version uses the Pokemon Go architecture — continuous GPS reported to a server that pushes 'a player is near you' — with Bluetooth/UWB only for the final face-to-face handshake. The concept is fun in principle, but its hardest problems aren't technical: it needs several players in the same small area at the same moment (a brutal local-density cold-start that has killed every comparable proximity-social app), and directing users toward real strangers creates a first-order safety and privacy burden.
businessCase.customer: Socially adventurous younger users (the Pokemon Go / experiential crowd) open to spontaneous real-world play with strangers — most realistically reached inside bounded, already-dense communities (a campus, festival, conference or event) rather than on the open street.
businessCase.market: Location-based gaming is a real but modest genre — roughly US$1.2B globally in 2023 (Japan alone ~US$620M, about half) — and it is dominated by games whose targets are virtual (Pokemon Go, Ingress), which sidesteps the need for another live player nearby. Pokemon Go's scale (1B+ downloads, ~US$1.9B peak-year revenue) is the wrong benchmark: its draw was ambient single-player-versus-environment play on pre-existing IP. A no-IP game whose targets are real people has a much smaller reachable market, and every comparable human-proximity social app has failed.
businessCase.model: Free-to-play with in-app purchases (power-ups, cosmetics, 'lures') and paid real-world events — the location-gaming norm — plus the more defensible path of selling the experience B2B to venues and event organisers (festivals, conferences, campuses, team-building) who supply the crowd.
businessCase.goToMarket: Density is the whole game, so a broad consumer launch would starve — the only viable start is to saturate one high-density, high-trust venue at a time (a single campus or a festival), prove the loop where players are already co-located and safety is bounded, then tile outward. Pokemon Go solved its own cold-start with global IP plus a pre-built map of points of interest from its earlier game; a startup has neither, and its 'points of interest' are live humans who must also be present.
businessCase.costs: Building a GPS-server MVP is modest, but there is no revenue until local density exists, and an app that directs users to real strangers needs identity/age verification, reporting/blocking, 'meet in public' guardrails and human moderation from day one — real cost and friction that work against the density it needs. Acquiring users in dense geographic clusters is expensive per active experience.
businessCase.risks: Two problems dominate. First, a two-sided local-density cold-start in its most acute form: the game is nothing unless another player is within a few metres right now — the exact failure that killed Color, Bump-style apps, Yik Yak and Zenly (the survivors either had huge IP or, like Happn's dating, a purpose valuable even at low density). Second, safety and liability: pointing users at real strangers to interact in person invites harassment, stalking and luring (location games already have a record of lure-based crime, and Yik Yak collapsed under cyberbullying), on top of a continuous-location privacy honeypot and Apple/Google limits on background location and Bluetooth. The RFID mechanic in the pitch also does not exist and must be dropped.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Drop 'RFID' — the buildable mechanic is GPS-to-server proximity with a Bluetooth/UWB foreground handshake. 2) Pick ONE bounded, dense, trusted venue (a campus, festival or conference) and prototype the loop there, where density is guaranteed and the crowd is closed — this also sidesteps the background-detection limits and most of the stranger-safety risk. 3) Design safety in from the start (opt-in, age-gating, reporting, public-space guardrails). 4) Validate that the core interaction (a 30-second rock-paper-scissors or code-word exchange with a nearby stranger) is actually fun and repeatable. 5) Only consider open-world consumer expansion after the bounded version proves it can manufacture density and stay safe.

clarifyingQuestions: Is this an open-world consumer app, or a bounded-venue experience (campus/festival/conference/team-building) sold B2B to the organiser? The bounded version dodges both the density cold-start and most of the safety risk — and is what can realistically ship.
How is the stranger-safety problem handled — age verification, reporting/blocking, public-space guardrails — given the core loop sends people to interact with strangers in person?
Who builds it? A reliable real-time geosocial game plus trust-and-safety infrastructure is a serious mobile-engineering effort the team would need to bring in.

ideas.title: Rotating-IP Projection Venue
ideas.oneLiner: A lower-capital immersive projection venue in Calgary running rotating licensed digital-art experiences — a 'chapter one' that could later upgrade toward a permanent build.

market.why: Immersive/projection entertainment has real, demonstrated pull — teamLab's Tokyo venues have drawn millions of visitors a year and touring shows have travelled widely, including through Calgary — but it is a volatile, boom-and-bust category and no reliable market-size figure could be verified. Treat demand as real but proven-cyclical, not a stable, sized market.

entry.why: Lower capital than a permanent narrative build (which runs into the tens of millions), and a licensed projection show is quick to stand up — but it still means a multi-year warehouse lease, a projector/media-server fit-out, and entering an oversupplied content space where the same shows are widely available.

cost.why: Capital-heavy and real-estate-committed: a projection-scale warehouse lease, projector array and media servers, plus recurring content-licensing fees and a relentless content-rotation treadmill to fight novelty fatigue. Below a permanent build's 8-figure cost, but not cheap, and the projection fit-out capex has no reliable public benchmark.

saturation.why: The touring projection-show space is oversupplied — a single subject (Van Gogh) spawned five or six competing shows in major cities on public-domain content, which drove the category's boom and bust. The permanent, proprietary end (Meow Wolf, teamLab) is genuinely uncontested in Canada, but that is not this licensed-projection model.

moat.why: The defining weakness. Licensed or public-domain content has no exclusivity — a licensor can sell the same or a rival show to anyone, including a competitor across town — so there is no content moat; differentiation must come from location, rotation cadence, events and hospitality, not the shows. The permanent-narrative model (proprietary, physically built) has a moat; this one does not.

margins.why: Ticketed admission (comparable touring shows ran ~US$25-75) against heavy fixed costs — lease, projection hardware, staffing — and novelty-limited runs that require constant, costly content refreshes. Margins are pressured by both oversupply and the rotation treadmill.

founderFit.why: Marketing and creative instinct fit the brand/experience and events side, and the team is in the target city — but no one has venue operations, immersive-content production or capital-project experience, and it is a capital-heavy real-estate commitment far from the team's leaner strengths.

risk.why: High, with a recent and direct precedent: the category's largest touring operator, Lighthouse Immersive (behind Immersive Van Gogh), went insolvent in 2023 — less than two years after the peak — undone by exactly this model's weaknesses of commodity content, oversupply and novelty fatigue. Add a multi-year real-estate commitment and no content moat, and the downside is a large, illiquid loss.

businessCase.summary: A lower-capital immersive venue in Calgary — a projection-and-interactive-room space running rotating licensed digital-art experiences, pitched as a 'chapter one' that could later upgrade toward a permanent Meow Wolf/teamLab-scale build. The appeal is real demand for immersive experiences (teamLab draws millions; touring shows have visited Calgary) and a genuine national white space at the permanent end (neither Meow Wolf nor teamLab has a Canadian location). But the licensed-projection version this describes has a defining flaw: the content is a commodity — a single subject like Van Gogh spawned five or six competing shows per city on public-domain material — so there is no moat, and the category's biggest touring operator, Lighthouse Immersive, went bankrupt in 2023 on exactly that dynamic. It is also a capital-heavy, real-estate-committed venue with no venue-operations capability on the team.
businessCase.customer: Calgary residents and visitors looking for a novel, weatherproof cultural outing — families, date-nights, tourists, and event/private-hire bookings — the audience touring immersive shows already draw locally.
businessCase.market: Immersive/projection entertainment has real, demonstrated pull (teamLab's Tokyo venues have drawn millions of visitors a year, and touring shows have visited Calgary), but it is a volatile, boom-and-bust category and no reliable market-size figure could be verified. The differentiated permanent end (Meow Wolf, teamLab) has no Canadian presence — a genuine white space — but the licensed-projection 'chapter one' competes in an oversupplied content space.
businessCase.model: Ticketed admission to timed immersive shows (comparable touring shows charged ~US$25-75), with rotating licensed content, plus events, private hires and a food-and-beverage attach to raise per-visit spend and drive repeat visits.
businessCase.goToMarket: Open a projection-scale space in a Calgary warehouse district, launch with a recognised licensed show to pull opening crowds, and sustain footfall through a rotating content calendar plus events and private hires. Position as the city's first permanent immersive venue, with an eventual upgrade path toward proprietary, built content.
businessCase.costs: A multi-year warehouse lease, projector array and media servers, and recurring content-licensing fees, plus the ongoing cost of rotating content to fight novelty fatigue. Below a permanent build's tens of millions, but capital-heavy and real-estate-committed, and the projection fit-out has no reliable public cost benchmark.
businessCase.risks: The content is a commodity with no exclusivity, so there is no moat and margins get competed away (the Van Gogh oversupply — five or six shows per city — is the pattern). Projection shows are largely one-and-done, forcing a costly content-rotation treadmill. The category's largest operator, Lighthouse Immersive, went insolvent in 2023. And it is a capital-heavy, multi-year real-estate bet the team has no venue-operations experience to run.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Confront the moat problem — a licensed-projection venue competes with anyone who licenses the same show; decide what (location, cadence, events, hospitality, or eventually proprietary content) makes it defensible. 2) Study why Lighthouse Immersive failed and what the survivors do differently. 3) Build the fit-out and lease capex bottom-up from real Calgary vendor/lease quotes (no public benchmark exists). 4) Model the content-rotation calendar and repeat-visit economics honestly. 5) Cover the venue-operations gap (hire or partner).

clarifyingQuestions: What makes it defensible, given a licensed or public-domain show can be run by any competitor — location, rotation cadence, events, hospitality, or an eventual move to proprietary content?
Given Lighthouse Immersive (Immersive Van Gogh) went bankrupt in 2023 on commodity content and novelty fatigue, what is different here?
Who runs the venue? This is capital-heavy hospitality/entertainment operations the team doesn't currently have.

ideas.title: In-city Nordic Thermal Spa
ideas.oneLiner: An in-city Nordic thermal spa and social bathhouse for Calgary — sauna, cold plunge and a hot-cold thermal cycle in the city itself, rather than the foothills day-trip Albertans currently drive to.

market.why: Genuine, structurally-supported demand. Contrast bathing (hot sauna, cold plunge) is a canonical wellness cycle rather than a fad, the urban social-bathhouse format is growing (Othership runs four urban venues in Toronto and New York), and the global wellness economy is large (~US$6.8T in 2024, a broad proxy). Calgary's cold climate and affluent population make year-round indoor thermal bathing a strong fit — the demand case is the strongest of Calgary's gap ideas.

entry.why: High barriers. A thermal spa is capital-heavy hospitality real estate — pools, multiple saunas, cold plunge, water treatment and heavy HVAC on a large urban footprint (Scandinave venues run 25,000-72,000 sq ft) — plus public-bathing water health-code regulation. Not a lean launch.

cost.why: Very capital-heavy and slow to pay back. The fit-out (water systems, saunas, plunge pools, HVAC) is a major upfront build with heavy ongoing utilities and maintenance, on a multi-year real-estate commitment. No reliable public build-cost benchmark was verifiable — model it bottom-up — but the scale is clearly high.

saturation.why: The urban social-bathhouse format is absent in Calgary (Othership and Scandinave have no Alberta location), so the in-city niche is open — but Alberta already has a destination Nordic spa (Kananaskis Nordic Spa, about an hour west) that owns the regional 'Nordic spa' mindshare as a day-trip, and the category is drawing new entrants.

moat.why: Modest. A prime urban location, a strong brand and a sticky membership base would be a real if unspectacular moat, but the format itself is replicable and a well-funded competitor could copy it. Location and membership loyalty are the defensible pieces.

margins.why: Premium pricing helps (destination day-passes run ~CAD$138-185; urban venues add memberships and drop-in sessions), but heavy fixed costs — utilities to continuously heat and chill water, maintenance, staff — and dependence on repeat-visit retention temper it.

founderFit.why: Marketing and community-building fit the brand side, and the team is in the target city — but no one has spa/hospitality operations, water-systems engineering or health-code experience, and it is a capital-heavy build far from the team's leaner, asset-light strengths.

risk.why: High, but with genuine demand behind it. The risks are capital intensity and a multi-year real-estate commitment, heavy ongoing utilities and maintenance, public-bathing water health-code regulation, competition from the established foothills destination spa, and dependence on membership retention (a beautiful venue people visit twice a year underperforms). The cold-climate demand fit contains the downside somewhat.

businessCase.summary: An in-city Nordic thermal spa and social bathhouse for Calgary — sauna, cold plunge and a hot-cold-rest thermal cycle located in the city, rather than the roughly hour-west foothills day-trip Albertans currently drive to (Kananaskis Nordic Spa). Demand is the strongest of Calgary's gap ideas: contrast bathing is a canonical wellness practice, the urban social-bathhouse format is growing (Othership runs four urban venues in Toronto and New York), the wellness economy is large, and Calgary's cold winters and affluent population make year-round indoor thermal bathing a natural fit — and no urban operator of this kind is in Calgary. The hard part is the build: it is capital-heavy hospitality real estate (pools, saunas, water treatment, HVAC on a 25,000-72,000 sq ft-scale footprint), health-code-regulated, retention-dependent, and needs hospitality-operations capability the team doesn't have.
businessCase.customer: Affluent, wellness-oriented Calgarians wanting frequent, convenient contrast-therapy and social bathing in the city — most valuably as members and regulars rather than occasional day-trippers — plus recovery-focused athletes and young professionals.
businessCase.market: Demand is genuine and structurally supported: contrast bathing is a canonical wellness cycle (not a fad), the urban social-bathhouse format is growing (Othership's four urban venues), and the global wellness economy is large (~US$6.8T in 2024, a broad proxy). Calgary's cold climate and high incomes make it a strong fit, and no urban Nordic bathhouse currently operates there — the existing option is the foothills destination spa about an hour west.
businessCase.model: Membership-led recurring revenue (a recovery/contrast-therapy club) plus premium drop-in sessions and day-passes (destination day-passes benchmark around CAD$138-185), with add-ons like massage and events. Frequency and membership retention drive the economics — which is what most differentiates an urban venue from the occasional-visit destination model.
businessCase.goToMarket: Open one urban venue in a central, accessible Calgary location and anchor revenue in memberships (convenience and frequency are the whole pitch versus the foothills day-trip), layering premium drop-ins and events on top. Lean on the wellness/recovery community and social content to build a regular base.
businessCase.costs: Capital-heavy: a large urban fit-out (pools, saunas, cold plunge, water treatment, heavy HVAC) on a multi-year lease or build, with substantial ongoing utilities, water-treatment and maintenance costs. No reliable public build-cost benchmark exists — it must be modelled bottom-up — but it is clearly a major upfront commitment with a long payback.
businessCase.risks: Capital intensity and a multi-year real-estate commitment; heavy ongoing utilities and maintenance; public-bathing water health-code regulation; competition from the established Kananaskis destination spa for regional 'Nordic spa' mindshare; and, above all, retention risk — an urban venue's economics depend on members coming frequently, not visiting twice a year. The team also lacks spa/hospitality-operations and water-systems experience.
businessCase.nextSteps: 1) Pin the build cost bottom-up from real Calgary contractor/fit-out quotes (no public benchmark exists) and size the capital honestly. 2) Validate the membership-frequency assumption — how often would Calgarians actually come, and at what price — since retention is make-or-break. 3) Scope Alberta public-bathing water health-code requirements early. 4) Differentiate clearly from the Kananaskis destination spa on convenience, frequency and social positioning. 5) Cover the spa/hospitality-operations gap (hire or partner with an experienced operator).

clarifyingQuestions: What capital envelope are we prepared to commit, given a thermal-spa fit-out (pools, saunas, water treatment, HVAC) is a major, long-payback build with no cheap version?
Will Calgarians visit often enough as members to carry an urban venue, versus the occasional day-trip to the foothills spa — what is the frequency and membership assumption?
Who runs it? This needs spa/hospitality operations and water-systems/health-code experience the team doesn't currently have.

ideas.title: Locality Game
ideas.oneLiner: A venue-bounded social icebreaker game for events: attendees' phones prompt quick real-world interactions with nearby participants, turning a conference, festival or team offsite into a networking game — sold B2B to the organiser.

market.why: Event technology is a real, growing host market — analyst estimates put event-management software in the ~US$8-24B range (differing scope) growing ~10% a year — and conference networking is a validated pain point (in one survey only 15% of organisers rated their event's networking 'very effective'). But the reachable slice for a proximity icebreaker game specifically is a niche feature within that market, not the whole of it.

entry.why: Far easier than an open-world consumer app. Selling one organiser reaches thousands of attendees at once, the event guarantees the player density the game needs, and a foreground, venue-bounded experience runs full-rate Bluetooth without fighting the iOS background-scanning throttles that cripple always-on proximity apps.

cost.why: Light. A foreground event app avoids the heavy consumer customer-acquisition spend (the organiser brings the crowd), and it can be sold per-event or as an organiser subscription — a comparable event game charges ~US$299 per experience — so time-to-revenue is short once the product exists.

saturation.why: Event gamification is already served — Whova ships a native 'Icebreaker Contest', Goosechase runs event scavenger hunts, and Brella/Grip/Swapcard all do AI networking/matchmaking. A real-time proximity peer-to-peer game appears unserved specifically, but it sits as an unbundled feature inside a category incumbents already occupy.

moat.why: Weak — this reads as a feature, not a company. The incumbents own the attendee's home screen (the official event app) and can bundle a proximity mini-game into software attendees already installed; Whova's existing icebreaker contest shows the intent. The only defensible edges are genuine gameplay depth or embedding into the existing platforms rather than competing with them.

margins.why: Event SaaS carries healthy software margins (a listed event-software comparable, Eventbrite, runs ~67-70% gross), but one-off per-event usage and event seasonality temper it; durable economics need repeat buyers on subscription (venues, agencies, conference series, corporate L&D).

founderFit.why: The team brings the build capability this most needs — in-house software-development and applied-AI capability, alongside marketing — so the mobile/event app is within reach, and the B2B-to-organiser sales motion suits its strengths. The remaining gaps are event-industry credibility and the reality that this stays a feature an incumbent platform could bundle.

risk.why: Materially lower risk than an open-world proximity game — the event guarantees player density (killing the cold-start) and the closed, opt-in, known-attendee crowd removes the stranger-safety problem. The remaining risks are commercial: it may be a feature incumbents bundle rather than a standalone company, event-app adoption is often cited at only ~30-40% of attendees (a proximity game is worthless below a density threshold in the room), usage can be one-off per event, and event demand is seasonal.

businessCase.summary: A social icebreaker game for live events: at a conference, festival, campus or corporate offsite, attendees who opt in are prompted by their phones to do quick real-world interactions with nearby participants — rock-paper-scissors, a code word, a challenge — turning networking into a game and helping shy attendees break the ice. It is the venue-bounded, B2B version of a proximity social game, sold to the event organiser. That framing fixes the problems that doom an open-world consumer version: the event guarantees the player density the game needs, the crowd is closed and opt-in (removing the stranger-safety risk), acquisition is cheap (sell one organiser, reach thousands), and a foreground venue-bounded app sidesteps the iOS limits on background proximity detection. The open question is defensibility — event platforms like Whova already ship icebreaker/gamification features and could bundle this into an app attendees have already installed, so it risks being a feature rather than a company.
businessCase.customer: Event organisers — conference and festival producers, universities, and corporate L&D/team-building buyers — who pay for tools that make attendee networking and engagement happen rather than leaving it to chance. Attendees are the players; the organiser is the buyer.
businessCase.market: Event technology is a multi-billion-dollar, roughly 10%-a-year market (analyst estimates range from ~US$8B to ~US$24B depending on scope), and networking is a recognised weak spot organisers actively try to fix (only 15% rate their event's networking 'very effective' in one survey). The reachable market for a proximity icebreaker game is a niche within this — most naturally a feature or module sold into the events and team-building budget.
businessCase.model: Organiser-side SaaS: per-event licences for one-off conferences and subscriptions for repeat buyers (venues, agencies, conference series, corporate L&D), mirroring how comparable event games price (from ~US$299 per experience up to a subscription). Software-style gross margins, but revenue quality depends on landing repeat/subscription buyers rather than one-off events.
businessCase.goToMarket: Sell to organisers, not consumers: land a few conferences, campuses or corporate offsites, prove the game lifts networking and engagement, and expand to repeat buyers and agencies. Because the event supplies the crowd, there is no consumer density to bootstrap. The sharpest wedge is the one thing incumbents don't do — real-time proximity peer-to-peer play — pursued deeply enough to matter before a platform copies it, or offered as an embeddable module to the existing event platforms.
businessCase.costs: Building a reliable foreground venue app plus the B2B sales motion are the main costs; there is no heavy consumer customer-acquisition spend because the organiser brings the crowd. The seasonality of events makes revenue lumpy under a per-event model.
businessCase.risks: The binding risk is defensibility: this reads as a feature, not a company — Whova already ships an 'Icebreaker Contest' and the major platforms bundle matchmaking and gamification into apps attendees already have, so an organiser may not buy a second app for one mechanic. Add adoption friction (event-app adoption is often cited at only ~30-40% of attendees, and a proximity game needs a threshold of active players in the room), one-off per-event usage, and event seasonality. The density and safety problems of a consumer proximity game are, however, largely solved by the venue-bounded framing.
